1:
The opening verb divides them. Ellicott says the expression is idiomatic and has no special force; Keil that it contributes to the pictorial character of the account and brings out its importance; Calvin that the Hebrews use it of undertaking any momentous matter. Ellicott rules out the literal sense of daughter, which the chronology makes impossible, and Keil and Wesley agree she was a descendant. Clarke alone takes it literally, that Jochebed was sister to Kohath and so both wife and aunt to Amram, such marriages being lawful then though afterwards forbidden, before allowing that descendant may be all it means. Calvin meets the chronology by grammar, preferring a pluperfect rendering, since otherwise the marriage would fall after the edict.

Ellicott turns the bareness of the notice into an argument: the simplicity here should be set beside the elaborate legends by which other religions surrounded their founders' births, Thoth, Zoroaster and Orpheus, and even the father's name is omitted, which he finds difficult to conceive of anyone but Moses doing. Clarke reads the silence otherwise, that since a new law was to be given and a new priesthood formed, God chose one religious family from which both lawgiver and high priest should spring. Henry adds that Jacob had left Levi under marks of disgrace, so that Moses springing from him typifies Christ, who came in the likeness of sinful flesh; and that when men are projecting the church's ruin God is preparing its salvation.

The child's beauty is variously weighed. Clarke says the Hebrew states only that he was good, which the Greek renders comely and Stephen comely to God, and that nothing interests the heart more than a lovely babe in distress, probably the sole motive that moved the princess. Ellicott adds Trogus Pompeius on his personal appearance, but insists the beauty must not be taken for the main cause of his mother's anxiety. Henry says they fancied in his countenance a lustre more than human, a specimen of the shining of his face long afterwards. Calvin faces the difficulty the others pass over, that the letter to the Hebrews ascribes the hiding to faith, and answers that faith and regard for beauty are almost contrary: had faith shone purely they would have cared nothing for his looks, so that the love his beauty awakened deservedly detracts from the praise of their faith, though God made the very impediment an assistant to prop their tottering belief.

Whether the parents acted well is the sharpest question, and Calvin stands alone. Five read the ark as careful contrivance: Keil that she hoped the child might be found by a compassionate hand, Ellicott that she laid it among the flags so it should not float out of sight, Clarke that she would not trust it to the stream and chose the spot the princess frequented, Wesley that God put it into their hearts so Moses might come into Pharaoh's daughter's hands, Gill that Miriam stood near enough to watch and far enough not to seem to belong to it. Calvin says instead that after three months the impulse of love passed and they almost abandoned him, that their timidity cannot advisedly be excused, and that since God gives even brute beasts so strong an instinct that the dam despises her life for her young, it is baser that men made in the divine image should be driven by fear to such inhumanity. He refuses the defence that they rested on providence, since it is a perversion to make providence an excuse for sloth, and asks what the ark was made and daubed for, if not to bury the child in it. On the sister, Ellicott makes Miriam fourteen or fifteen and credits her with much quickness, where Gill reports ten or twelve, and some seven; Calvin thinks she was stationed rather to witness her brother's murder than to secure his safety.
5:
What the princess came to the river to do is disputed, and Clarke fights on three fronts. The word for herself is not in the original, he observes, so there was no bathing but the washing of clothes, which even kings' daughters did not think beneath them; he sets the scene beside Homer's Nausicaa washing her brothers' garments at the shore and calls the two almost parallels. He rejects Harmer's theory of a ritual plunge at the Nile's rising; dismisses the Targum's tale of ulcers healed on touching the ark; and calls Josephus's version, with the ark borne off by the current and a swimmer sent after it, a fable and not even a cunningly devised one. Ellicott takes the bathing as it stands and defends it from Egyptian custom, women there having great liberty and Nile water being reckoned healthy, the princess using a part reserved for women.

On her name the tradition is threefold: Gill gives Thermuthis from Josephus, Merrhis from Artapanus, which he thinks borrowed from Miriam, and Bithia from the Jewish writers, which he suspects lifted from another Pharaoh's daughter. Why the child was not nursed by an Egyptian is answered two ways. Gill reports from Jarchi, Josephus and the Talmud that he refused the breast of several Egyptian women, which gave Miriam her opening, and Clarke the same; Ellicott reconstructs it without the legend, that the princess must have shown her intention before Miriam dared speak, and that Miriam half divines and half anticipates her thought.

The name Moses divides them philologically. Ellicott makes it Egyptian, the Mesu of nineteenth-dynasty monuments, common as the second half of such names as Ra-mesu, meaning born or son but derived from a verb meaning to draw forth, on which the princess justified it, a play transferring exactly into Hebrew. Keil also insists it must be Egyptian since an Egyptian gave it, reporting Josephus that the Egyptians call water Mo and those rescued from it Uses, and that Coptic confirms this though Josephus gives another account elsewhere. Clarke keeps it Hebrew, the verb signifying to draw out and the name meaning the person drawn out, and confesses we do not know what name his parents gave him. Wesley reports that his father called him Joachim.

Calvin cares nothing for etymology and everything for the irony. The king's daughter did not give the name without the preventing Spirit of God, he says, so that whenever Moses heard it he must remember of what people he sprang; she could by no means have intended this and would rather have had his origin forgotten, but God, who put words in the mouth of Balaam's ass, moved her tongue to bear public testimony to the very thing she would have preferred to conceal. He adds that the parents' grief was renewed when the child was torn as it were from their bowels, and wonders that Moses kept his integrity in so corrupting a court. Ellicott doubts the adoption was formal, since we have no evidence yet that adoption was an Egyptian custom, and thinks the writer may mean only that she brought him up as a son; he reconstructs that upbringing as no more than a prince's education, the cursive and not the hieroglyphic character reserved to priests, and letter-writing as the most necessary gentlemanlike accomplishment. Wesley makes that education threefold and providential, fitting Moses to be a prince, an historian and an ambassador to that very court in God's name, and finds in a Jewish lawgiver bearing an Egyptian name a happy omen for the Gentile world. Keil accounts for the princess's pity by the love of children innate in her sex, and quotes Augustine that the murderer of infants was fitly punished through his own affections. Henry adds that God often raises friends for his people among their enemies, and that never did poor child cry so seasonably.
11:
Going out is taken by three as renunciation. Ellicott says it is no mere visit but a complete withdrawal from the palace, the first sign of that sympathy for his people which culminates in the cry that God should blot him out of his book. Calvin says he withdrew privately, preferring enmity to concealing his affection, and came not only to pity their estate but to share their lot. Henry makes the point from Hebrews, that he reckoned it more his honour to be a son of Abraham than of Pharaoh's daughter. Keil neither praises nor blames, observing only that the court education could not extinguish the feeling that he belonged to Israel, and that the narrative never tells us how a feeling nourished by his mother's milk grew into a settled will, but only how it broke forth in the full-grown man.

On the silent years Ellicott and Clarke go opposite ways. Ellicott finds it remarkable that Moses tells us nothing of his youth, and dismisses the later traditions as worthless. Clarke retails one from Josephus: when the Ethiopians had overrun much of Egypt an oracle advised employing Moses, who was made general, drove them back and besieged them in Saba, and Tharbis, the Ethiopian king's daughter, fell desperately in love with him and promised to surrender the city if he would marry her, which he did; Stephen, Clarke thinks, alluded to something of this kind in calling Moses mighty in deeds as well as words. On his age all defer to Stephen: Gill reports that some Jewish writers say eighteen and others twenty, but holds Stephen most to be credited at forty.

Whether the killing was lawful is the chapter's sharpest division, and Ellicott stands alone. He says the Jewish commentators gloss the act over or even eulogise it as heroical, but that it was clearly the deed of a hasty and undisciplined spirit: the offence did not deserve death, and had it done so Moses had neither legal office nor divine call to make himself an executioner, so that by this one wrong act he lost forty years of usefulness to his brethren. The others justify him by commission. Calvin holds that Stephen witnesses Moses was not impelled by rash zeal but knew himself divinely appointed avenger, and was armed by God's command. Clarke supplies a ground nobody else has, that the Egyptian had probably killed the Hebrew, so that Moses was justified on the precept given to Noah. Wesley and Henry say the same shorter, that he acted by special warrant from heaven.

Yet the two who defend him most also fence the defence about. Calvin draws the limit: private persons are by no means countenanced by this example if they repress wrong by force, since the sword of vengeance belongs to the judges, and if these will not aid the innocent, all we can do is murmur. Wesley makes the same reservation in a parenthesis, that the warrant makes no precedent in ordinary cases. Calvin also refuses to call the act perfect: the looking about, and the daring not to strike except by a secret blow, show that Moses was not so bold as he should have been and his faith was weak, so that the Apostle's praise must not be read as praise of something perfect. Gill reads the same glance the other way, as arguing no consciousness of evil but only care for his own preservation, lest being seen he be accused to Pharaoh. Ellicott closes with a note that doubles as an argument about the writer: east of the Delta the sand creeps close to the cultivated ground, and Moses naturally remembered digging the grave in the sand, where any other writer would have said in the ground. Wesley adds the tradition that he used no weapon but slew him with the word of his mouth, as Peter slew Ananias.
13:
The second day brings Moses back, and the voices notice that he no longer acts as a judge. Calvin makes the return the proof of resolve: it shows he was firm in abandoning the Court, the tyrant's violence being no obstacle to a man whom hope of future recompense made superior to present fear. But he does not assume, as before, the character of a judge; he performs the duty charity demands of everyone, reproving moderately, wishing not to reproach the offender with his fault but to calm his ferocity. Ellicott agrees from the wording: the Hebrew calls the man simply the wicked one, and though Acts reports the speech differently, in either case there was no offensive assumption of authority, and the wrongdoer took offence anyway. Clarke turns from the two men to the Church, finding it strange that where they suffered persecution as Hebrews they should persecute each other, as the oppressed Church has repeatedly divided over unessential points of doctrine and so become easy prey.

The rejoinder is read three ways. Wesley takes it as the standing fate of reproof: a friendly reproof needs no great authority and is an act of kindness, yet this man will interpret it an act of dominion, as people sick of good discourse call it preaching. Gill grants a narrower point, that God had designed Moses for a prince and so he afterwards appeared, but he was not appointed by Pharaoh, and had only persuaded them to peace as brethren. Ellicott alone makes the exchange forensic, and collects the bill for the previous day: no one had given Moses jurisdiction, and he had interfered as any man of position naturally interferes to stop a quarrel. Here is the sting of the rejoinder; here was the assumption of authority, not in the interposition of to-day but in the blow of yesterday. That fatal error laid him open to attack and deprived him of the influence as a peacemaker.

On the temper that answers correction Calvin is fullest, and reaches for an anvil. Whoever restrains the wicked must expect such indignities; from the petulance of one man we learn how perverse the whole nation was, which is why Stephen accuses them all of ingratitude; and the nature God has not tamed repels correction as firmly as an anvil repels a hammer. He notes the cowardice under the insolence: the slave who would not dare murmur at a blow from the lowest Egyptian rages imperiously here, threatening the man he should have received as an angel of God.

The flight raises the chapter's one exegetical knot, and Clarke unties it. How can Moses fleeing for fear be reconciled with the word that by faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the king's wrath? Very easily: the apostle speaks not of this flight but of the final departure. Calvin concedes the fear, saying his zeal was mingled with infirmity yet prevailed, and finds the firmness in his refusing to appease the king and choosing exile; God in a manner withdrew him, and the Desert may well be called his school. Ellicott states the law flatly: nothing reduced the crime from murder to manslaughter, and the motives which excuse it to moderns would not have moved a Pharaoh. Wesley reads the delay as providence, Egypt's iniquity not being full nor Israel yet humbled, and thinks Midian chosen because its people were of Abraham's seed and kept the true worship. Clarke reports the descent disputed: the line runs from Abraham by Keturah through Midian to Raguel and Jethro, but Calmet, on the ground of Miriam's reproach of the Cushite wife, derives them from Cush the son of Ham. Ellicott ends on an article: not a well but the well, one principal copious well generally resorted to. Wesley leaves him there tired and thoughtful, though but the other day he was at ease in Pharaoh's court.
16:
Calvin opens on providence: the profane would attribute this meeting to good fortune, whereas God affords in it a striking picture of his providence, directing his servant's steps with an outstretched hand to a home that lasted out his exile. What Reuel was is disputed. Clarke says the word means priest or prince or both. Gill reports the Targums and the heathen Artapanus rendering it prince, but prefers priest with Aben Ezra, since otherwise Moses would hardly have married into the house. Ellicott takes him for a priest on the strength of his later sacrifices, and notes that Reuel means friend of God. Calvin argues from the Arabic root, one who draws nigh, and rejects prince on a domestic ground: a rich man would not have been without servants, and so would not have exposed his daughters daily to the quarrels of shepherds.

Calvin then grades the Midianite religion rather than sorting it, where Ellicott had said flatly that they worshipped the true God. Moses could scarcely have married into a house defiled by foul unrighteousness, yet it is plain elsewhere that they were joined to idols. His resolution is that there is some difference between idolatry and the impure worship of God, and that these had not entirely departed from its principles, though they had contracted some defilement from the stinking puddles of error which had gradually crept in.

At the well Clarke settles a grammatical question: the verb is masculine, so the shepherds drove off the flocks and not the daughters, watering their own cattle from the troughs the women had filled. Ellicott supplies the custom that was broken, the rule of the desert being that those who come to a well take their turns in order of arrival; and he infers from Reuel's surprise that they are come so soon that the rudeness was habitual. He also reads Moses as changed: again the champion of the oppressed, but taught by the past, so that he uses no unnecessary violence. Henry draws the daughters instead, humble, industrious and modest, since they would not ask the stranger home till their father sent for him.

The father's name defeats everyone. Clarke lists Reuel, Raguel, Jethro, Hobab and Keni, blaming the letter ayin, which scarcely any European organs can enunciate. Calvin makes three generations of it, Reuel the grandfather, Jethro the father, Hobab the brother, arguing from age that the old man returned home from the desert while Hobab stayed to be instead of eyes. Wesley agrees in a line, and Gill reports the Targum of Jonathan's father's father only to say it does not follow.

Henry and Wesley make the exile a curriculum. Egypt accomplished Moses as scholar, gentleman, statesman and soldier, but he lacked one thing the court could not give; by the former he was prepared to rule in Jeshurun, by the latter to converse with God in Horeb. Calvin will not let the forty years be comfortable: the flower of his age was past and his strength failing, so that his vocation might seem obsolete and abrogated, and it is God's grace that kept him calm and daily prepared. Keil observes only that it pleased Moses to dwell there, the verb meaning that he was willing, and that the life was still banishment. On the son's name Ellicott gives ger and sham, with Jerome's advena ibi; Gill calls it desolate stranger, but not by way of complaint; Calvin rejects the reading of it as a name of congratulation, holding that Moses called strange the land where he had found a peaceful home, and declared himself a sojourner wherever he dwelt until he should obtain the promised inheritance. Ellicott collects two more traits for Mosaic authorship: that the girls said an Egyptian where any other writer would have said a man, and that Moses had to draw water enough because the shepherds had used some of theirs.
23:
Who the dead king was is worked at from four directions. Ellicott argues from regnal length: Moses was eighty at the Exodus and forty when he quitted Egypt, so the Pharaoh he fled from must have reigned above forty years, and only Thothmes the Third and Rameses the Second reigned so long in that stretch of dynasties. Clarke names candidates instead, reporting Usher for Ramesses Miamun, whose son Amenophis drowned in the Red Sea, and Abul Farajius for Amenophis himself. Gill sets Eusebius against Usher, the one giving Orus, Acenchres and Achoris, the other making this the king under whom Moses was born, dead in the sixty-seventh year of his reign; and Gill cautions that things are often put close together in Scripture which were done at a considerable distance. Calvin reasons from what is usual: the tyrant of the first chapter can hardly have lived so long, since he would then have reigned above eighty years, so one or more kings came between, which is Wesley's guess too.

Why the cry comes now, after so many silent years, is the question the pastoral voices care about. Calvin denies that the grief was new: they did not then first begin to lament, but became more alive to their woes, since hope of a kinder successor had softened their misery, and when the change of kings lightened nothing their sorrow increased and forced them to cry out more loudly. He presses it into a rule about prayer: they had looked in other directions until all earthly means were cut off, and were then forcibly drawn to seek help from above, so that our prayers are not straightway directed to God, and much is required to stimulate our sluggish hearts. Ellicott says the same historically, that they had expected a new king to initiate a new policy, or at least signalise his accession by a remission of burdens, and he did neither. Henry and Wesley make it a return, that now at last they began to think of God and to turn from the idols they had served, having hitherto fretted at the instruments of their trouble while God was not in all their thoughts; and both draw the same sign, that God is coming with deliverance when he inclines us to cry to him for it.

On the infanticide the same two are alone in noticing that it has quietly stopped. Probably the murdering of infants did not continue, they say, that part of the affliction attending only the birth of Moses to signalise it; the Egyptians were now content with their increase, finding Egypt enriched by their labour, so that they cared not how many slaves they had. Gill takes the notice of the king's death to show only that it made no alteration in their afflictions for the better, but rather the worse.

The four verbs of the last two verses are handled as accommodations. Clarke says God's covenant is God's engagement, and his remembering it means only that he now began to give it effect. Calvin explains the word by its contrary: God is said to forget when he does not really and openly appear and stretch forth his hand to help, so that both expressions have relation to effect. Keil reaches the same place through Lyra's gloss, that God behaved after the manner of one who knows, by showing love toward them, and Luther's plain paraphrase, He accepted them. Gill and Clarke agree that knew here means approved. Clarke adds a textual note: for God in the last clause Houbigant reads upon them, a difference of two letters, countenanced by the Vulgate, Septuagint, Chaldee, Coptic and Arabic; our translators insert unto them for the same sense. Henry counts the four namings of God and calls the effect a work worthy of God, the covenant and not any merit of theirs being what he had an eye to.
